# Applications: Wearable Technology: From the Practice Field to Prime Time (SSAC16)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Set an individual exposure ceiling for athletes returning from soft tissue injury (hamstring first), using the same logic as the Browns hamstring "pitch count" [08:42]. At Baylor this means a per-athlete cap on high-speed running or sprint exposure in Catapult for the weeks after a return, agreed with Athletic Medicine and reviewed against the athlete's status, not a team-wide number.
- Inference: Use a jump or landing count for volleyball and basketball athletes with a lower-limb history, as the Florida volleyball staff did with a jump count [06:06]. The decision is whether a count from the device replaces a hand tally by a student trainer, which the coach said did not work well.
- Inference: Build a weekly "scale back" rule from the Hawkins story of legs feeling worst on game day [09:44]: compare mid-week Catapult load with a next-morning or game-day readiness marker (for example the daily CMJ metric already collected) and look for athletes where high game-day fatigue repeats.
- Inference: Write down a staff rule for how wearable output may and may not be used in roster decisions, using the panel's split between "keep players honest" misuse and career-long management [14:55]. This governs what a position coach is allowed to ask for from Applied Performance reports.
- Inference: Decide what athletes can see of their own data. The player on the panel reports that early NFL players removed the devices when they were not shown their data [37:57]; a Baylor athlete-facing view is a retention question for the monitoring program.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: the technology stack is Catapult for GPS with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system. The talk agrees that Catapult is a standard tool; it adds nothing on how Baylor uses it.
- Eric's baseline: the course material describes a "culture of fear" that grew out of early GPS and load work, pushing teams to under-train in the name of recovery (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk partly agrees: the Catapult panelist says the worst use is policing effort [14:25], and the coach says the data confirms what she already thought rather than overriding her [08:11]. It does not address under-training directly.
- Eric's baseline: no sport-specific or position-specific GPS thresholds exist in the data dictionary, named as unfinished work (Explicit). The talk extends this only weakly: it argues for personalized rather than uniform loads [11:50] but gives no thresholds.
- Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost against insight, and daily subjective surveys were dropped for objective force-plate data. The talk agrees on context: data alone does not say what to do next [25:38].
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supplies information to support Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions rather than making return-to-performance calls (Explicit). The talk agrees: the coach says medical staff decide on concussion removal [33:21].

## What would have to be true

- Per-athlete caps need a baseline of that athlete's own recent exposure, so several weeks of clean Catapult data per athlete before the cap means anything.
- Injury mechanism and timing need to be recorded (practice versus game, sprinting versus decelerating) or a count of "soft tissue injuries" cannot be matched to exposure. The Australian rule-change example needed a year of velocity data and injury counts side by side [30:45].
- A readiness marker needs to exist for the same athletes on the same days as the load data.
- Athletic Medicine has to agree to any return-phase cap before it is used.

## Do not apply when

- The claim is about the evidence base. The 83 percent soft tissue figure is credited by the Catapult panelist to a college coach in the captions [17:58], and the Australian rule example is described as a correlation over one year [31:17]. Neither is a controlled test, so do not use either as a target effect size.
- The speakers include a vendor executive (Catapult), a chip maker, and a neurostimulation founder; adoption numbers and the "ubiquitous in three to five years" forecast are commercial views [18:30].
- Pro examples (guaranteed Australian contracts, NFL mileage affecting draft position [39:58]) do not transfer to college eligibility and scholarship rules without checking Baylor and NCAA policy.
- The volleyball jump-count example had no stated evidence on the right number; the coach and Intel panelist both note that the sport lacks data on how many jumps are too many [23:37]. A cap set without that is a guess.
- Small squads and single-athlete cases: a hamstring pitch count on one player shows nothing about whether the cap was the cause.

## First step

- Inference: Pull one position group's Catapult high-speed running totals for the last full season next to the dates of soft tissue injuries, in a throwaway sheet, to see whether the exposure data and the injury log can be lined up at all. Change nothing in practice yet.

- Athletic Medicine has to agree to any return-phase cap before it is used.

## Do not apply when

- The claim is about the evidence base. The 83 percent soft tissue figure is credited by the Catapult panelist to a college coach in the captions [17:58], and the Australian rule example is described as a correlation over one year [31:17]. Neither is a controlled test, so do not use either as a target effect size.
- The speakers include a vendor executive (Catapult), a chip maker, and a neurostimulation founder; adoption numbers and the "ubiquitous in three to five years" forecast are commercial views [18:30].
- Pro examples (guaranteed Australian contracts, NFL mileage affecting draft position [39:58]) do not transfer to college eligibility and scholarship rules without checking Baylor and NCAA policy.
- The volleyball jump-count example had no stated evidence on the right number; the coach and Intel panelist both note that the sport lacks data on how many jumps are too many [23:37]. A cap set without that is a guess.
- Small squads and single-athlete cases: a hamstring pitch count on one player shows nothing about whether the cap was the cause.

## First step

- Inference: Pull one position group's Catapult high-speed running totals for the last full season next to the dates of soft tissue injuries, in a throwaway sheet, to see whether the exposure data and the injury log can be lined up at all. Change nothing in practice yet.

- Inference: Hold coach ratings in a consistent format. The validation depended on coaches rating players on about 24 dimensions after a year [09:54]; a Baylor staff could collect a smaller version at the end of each season, which is the data any future validation would need.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: favor a small number of valid, reliable tests over an exhaustive battery, and repeat them identically over time (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees on validation: it insists the measure be tied to an outcome before use [08:52], though it adds a test of a different kind (psychological).
- Eric's baseline: data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance and staff attention, and a valid test can still be the wrong choice operationally (Explicit). The talk's one-hour, 100 percent participation test at the combine [07:20] shows a case where the cost was accepted; Baylor has no equivalent captive setting.
- Eric's baseline: a trained "coach's eye" matters as much as any technology (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk does not conflict: its validation target is the coaches' own ratings [09:54].
- No direct link found for personality or intelligence testing; the baseline has no psychological assessment content.

- A validated instrument and a legal review. The speakers are industrial and organizational psychologists with litigation backgrounds [08:21]; a college program would need permission and policy review, not a homemade survey.

- A rule for how the result is used: the speakers present it as an addition to physical evidence, not a substitute [06:17].

- The ratings are the only outcome. Coaches' ratings after a year may reflect the same impressions the test is meant to predict; the talk shows penalties and a small injury relationship as other criteria [17:07], [17:37], but gives no detail.
- The athletes are 17 to 19 year olds with no pro-level selection. The talk's evidence is NFL combine participants, a different population.
- A cluster or "bust rate" is used to rule out an individual. The cluster outputs are group rates (for example 41 percent and 83 percent below the "bust" line [24:19]) and the speakers describe the approach as lowering risk, not predicting individuals.
- The result would reach recruits or athletes as a label. The speakers are describing a league-run process for professionals.

## First step

- Inference: List which non-physical items Baylor coaches already rate informally (learning speed, dependability, leadership) and write them as a single short rubric with a 1 to 5 scale. Use it on the current roster for one position group and file the results with no decision attached.

# Applications: Quantifying Injury Risk, presented by Kitman Labs (SSAC17)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Check Baylor's own load flags against Baylor's own injury log before using them to hold athletes back. The talk's central example is a team that held athletes back after a one standard deviation jump in high-speed running, while its injuries clustered at low exposure [07:43]. A Baylor version is to plot the weekly Catapult count (high-speed running, accelerations, decelerations) against the next-week injury rate for football only.
- Inference: Test whether the published acute to chronic ratio line of 1.5 [10:43] fits Baylor's data before using it as a red flag. The talk found it did not fit any of four rugby teams in one league.
- Inference: Split practice from game when computing risk. The speaker says game injuries per exposure run far higher than training injuries and that pooling inflates the practice risk figure [17:18]. This affects any risk number shown to coaches.
- Inference: Record injury mechanism and phase (acceleration versus deceleration, for example in hamstring injuries) in the athletic medicine log, since the talk argues the question has to be specific to the pathology [17:49].
- Inference: Treat the talk's availability-weighted-by-salary idea as a framing for staff, not a method. A Baylor equivalent would weight lost days by role (starter versus depth) when reporting football availability.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: the central athlete-management system is Kitman Labs (Explicit), so the speaker's company is the vendor in Baylor's stack. The talk is Kitman's own account of its work, so treat its claims as vendor claims.
- Eric's baseline: a "culture of fear" grew out of load monitoring and pushed teams to under-train (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees strongly: its examples show more injuries at lower exposure for a soccer team and two NFL teams [06:42], [08:13].
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine (course team position). The talk extends this by quantifying a team-specific risk range, and adds a view that risk tolerance can change by roster and week [13:14].
- Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model such as acute to chronic ratio is attributed to Eric, and the ACWR material in the corpus is reference only. The talk conflicts with using a fixed ratio threshold at all; the baseline takes no position.
- Eric's baseline: no sport-specific or position-specific GPS thresholds exist yet (Explicit gap). The talk extends this: it argues thresholds are team-specific and should be derived from local data [10:13].

## What would have to be true

- Enough injuries of one type to build any model. The speaker states that a typical Premier League team has few comparable injuries per year [12:14]; a single football roster has the same problem, so expect to describe, not predict.
- Consistent injury coding with mechanism, timing and practice versus game status.
- Load data with matching dates and athlete IDs so exposure can be lined up with injury.
- Athletic Medicine agreement before any exposure number is used to change training.

## Do not apply when

- The claim concerns the salary-based wins link. It uses base salary as a stand-in for contribution and reports 0.76 for the NBA and 0.89 for the NFL [03:08]; salary cap and contract structure do not exist in college, so the percent-of-wins figures [04:40] have no Baylor equivalent.
- The injury counts are small. The talk's own point about sample size [12:14] applies to a single roster.
- Someone proposes raising loads on the strength of the "less work, more injuries" charts. The speaker says the shape is reversed only in some teams and some metrics; at 200 accelerations the NFL example went the other way [08:43].
- The product claims are used as targets: the 42 percent reduction in days lost and the 25-league footprint are company statements [19:21], [19:51] with no method shown in the captions.
- Any mention of machine learning or "forecasting" is treated as available. The speaker says it is a direction, not a finished capability [12:44].

## First step

- Inference: Export last season's football injury log and weekly Catapult totals into one sheet and mark each injury with its week's exposure relative to that athlete's own average. Look at the chart before deciding anything.

=== FILE: videos/2016-04-30_F6MdSucj8J4_wearable-technology-from-the-practice-field-to-prime-time-pr/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: F6MdSucj8J4
title: "SSAC16: Wearable Technology: From the Practice Field to Prime Time (Presented by Catapult)"
event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Mary wise (caption spelling), Steve Holmes, Andrew Hawkins, adieu schiffman (caption spelling), Daniel Chao, Abe matkour (caption spelling, moderator)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, american-football, policy, other-sport:volleyball]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated panel with a college volleyball coach, an Intel manager, an NFL receiver, a Catapult executive and a neurostimulation founder on wearables in team sport. The panelists argue that player welfare comes first and that performance, fan engagement and broadcast value follow from it. Practical examples include jump counts for volleyball, a hamstring "pitch count" for a Browns player, and an Australian rule change tied to late-game velocity. The recurring cautions are that data needs context, should not drive cut decisions alone, and raises unresolved questions about who owns player data in collective bargaining. Claims are mostly anecdotes and company views.

## Key claims

- The Catapult speaker frames practice and game day as one continuum, with wearables serving player welfare, tactics, broadcast and fans [03:35].
- Florida's volleyball staff turned to a jump-measuring wearable after a hand-tracked jump limit for an injured player worked poorly [06:06].
- The coach uses it daily to see when front-row players reach diminishing returns and to adjust drills; she says it confirms her judgment and adds objective feedback [07:39], [08:11].
- Hawkins says a Browns player with hamstring trouble was put on a "pitch count" and then played all 16 games [08:42], [09:13].
- Hawkins says scaled-back weekly work lets athletes peak on Sunday, supported by data rather than by his own report of tired legs [09:44].
- The Catapult speaker says soft tissue injuries should not be treated as acceptable and that welfare is the base of the whole ecosystem [10:16].
- Training personalization is named as a major opportunity, since a uniform workload suits one athlete and overloads another [11:50].
- Hawkins expects resistance once data feeds evaluation, because it may shorten some careers while extending others [13:22], [13:53].
- The Catapult speaker says the worst use is policing effort, and says he has seen no evidence of players cut for falling scores [14:25], [14:55]. Hawkins disagrees from experience of players cut despite good play [15:25].
- Data should be contextualized and complementary to human judgment [16:55].
- A panelist notes that volleyball has little research on how many jumps are too many, and that research has mostly been on men [22:03], [22:35].
- For fan engagement, the Catapult speaker says people want stories, not raw data [24:07].
- Next-level analytics should say what to do next, not only report what happened [25:08], [25:38].
- Catapult speaker: Australian football used wearable data to test a substitution rule change; late-quarter velocity and soft tissue injuries fell together [30:45], [31:17].
- On concussion, the Halo founder says prevention is best and that stimulation after concussion would need a clinical trial [31:48], [32:18].
- The coach says concussion removal belongs to medical staff [33:21].
- The panel disagrees on collective bargaining: Hawkins expects data access and public disclosure to come up in the next agreement; the Catapult speaker says unions should be involved [36:56], [37:57].
- In Australia, a player's data follows a trade; Hawkins expects NFL workload history to follow players and affect draft and signing outcomes [38:58], [39:58].
- A Catapult speaker says wearable data is handled much like medical data (HIPAA compliance), with gaps in athlete access [49:10]; another panelist says performance and medical data should be blended [50:44].
- A closing criterion offered: data should connect to value, be non-obvious and be actionable [57:19].
- Hawkins predicts a new talent pool of people who translate data [58:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Jump count limit for the injured player: 40 jumps in a week, set by doctors [06:06].
- A volleyball player jumps over 11 feet 3 inches and averages over 30 inches in practice [07:08].
- Browns hamstring case: 16 games played; three or four earlier seasons with large missed time [09:13].
- Catapult works with 800 to 900 teams ("eight or nine hundred") [14:25].
- Catapult business size: from 50 or 60 million dollars to 300 million dollars in a year [17:58].
- Elite-market penetration: seven, eight or nine percent, and "under 10" percent [17:58], [18:30]. Forecast of near-universal use in three to five years [18:30].
- Claimed 83 percent drop in soft tissue injuries credited to a college coach (caption spelling "Jimbo official FSU") [17:58].
- Average NFL career: three years, which wearables could help extend to six (Hawkins) [13:22].
- Catapult high school clients: under two dozen [21:02].
- Snowboarding landings of 10 G's versus 20 G's shown on a broadcast [20:02].
- Softball and volleyball serve speeds of 55 to 65 miles an hour mentioned as a wearable target [27:40].
- Catapult future focus "70" on predictive analytics (caption is garbled; unit not stated) [54:45].
- Hawkins: NFL workload tracked for the eight years since high school [39:58].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable accelerometer-based tracking (Catapult, the vert jump sensor); tackle identification through algorithms from sensor data, since no single sensor flags a tackle [29:14].
- Load limits by count (jumps, hamstring reps) set with trainers.
- Australian football rule test: measure velocity and soft tissue injury frequency over a season of use [30:45], [31:17].
- Biometric data used to see different performance and injury risk in wet and dry weather [42:30].
- Active (neurostimulation) versus passive (sensing) wearables [46:06].
- Virtual reality for quarterback reps without physical load [47:07].

## Limits and open questions

- No sample sizes, controls or data are shown. Injury-reduction claims are single stories or vendor statements.
- Four of six speakers have a commercial stake (Catapult, Intel, Halo, plus the sport-technology framing).
- The Australian rule-change result is called a direct correlation over a year; cause is the speaker's reading.
- Speakers disagree on whether data is used to cut players; no evidence is shown either way.
- Captions do not reliably separate speakers in places; "Mary wise," "adieu schiffman," "Abe matkour," the introducer's name and several product names are probably misspelled.
- The caption at [56:17] reads "will not be solid" where the intended word may be different.

## Q&A

- High school adoption: Catapult sees uptake starting; challenge is simplification, not hardware [21:02], [24:37].
- Past data for data's sake: stories and "what next" recommendations [24:07], [25:38].
- Wanted wearable: ball speed on the wrist (coach); concussion detection and a first-down ball sensor (Hawkins) [27:10], [28:12].
- Concussion prevention and treatment [31:48].
- Pulling a player at the end of a final game on wearable data [32:50].
- Accuracy, battery life and security [34:23], [34:54].
- Collective bargaining and data ownership [35:56].
- Licensing heart rate for broadcast [40:29].
- Weather as data [41:30].
- Protecting college and high school athletes' data, and treating it as medical information [48:40], [49:10].
- Fashion and consumer wearables [51:14], [53:15].
- Where things stand in two years [55:15].

topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported

status: draft
---

## Summary

Two industrial and organizational psychologists describe a one-hour psychological assessment given to every player at the NFL combine since 2013. It measures cognitive ability and personality traits tied to football, and is meant as an addition to physical and film evidence. A three-year validation study compared combine scores with coach ratings of players after at least a year, plus penalties and injuries. Correlations are modest (about 0.22 to 0.35) but the speakers show that top and bottom scorers are rated very differently. The second half describes player-type clusters, a bust-rate comparison using a public value metric, and planned longitudinal modeling of second contracts.

## Key claims

- The goal was to add a standardized psychological measure alongside combine physical tests, not to replace them [04:13], [06:17].
- A league study with team executives produced 16 factors, with intelligence and personality as the two key areas [05:46].
- Intelligence items cover learning, thinking quickly and avoiding mental errors; personality items cover leadership, teamwork, self-control, dependability, preparedness and team fit [06:50].
- The test has run at the combine since 2013 with full participation, and the data were also turned into a coaching report [07:20], [07:51].
- The validation compared pre-draft scores with coach ratings after the players had been on a team for at least a year [09:54].
- The speaker calls correlations of this size good for behavioral science and says they are uncorrected [10:24].
- High, middle and low test scores matched coach rating bands; coaches were more straightforward than expected [12:27], [12:59].
- Low scorers on intelligence were about three times as likely to be rated poor as star; high scorers about three times as likely rated star [13:30].
- Personality: low scorers were about four times as likely to be rated low, high scorers about four and a half times as likely rated high [14:32].
- Intelligence and personality together predicted some ratings better, such as decisions under stress [15:33], [16:03].
- Decisions under stress also correlated with penalties per play and yards per penalty, and the result held in a larger sample [16:35], [17:07].
- Personality variables relate to injuries only weakly, with significance, in an early study; injury type has not been examined [17:37], [18:07].
- Cluster analysis found nine player types combining coach-rated physical talent and the psychological scores [22:16].
- A "whole package" cluster had a lower bust rate than a low-on-everything cluster, and two clusters with opposite strengths had the same failure rate [24:19], [25:20].
- The speakers argue this approach can find undervalued players and de-risk draft and contract decisions [25:51].
- Planned work: longitudinal models for second-contract decisions [26:53], [27:24].

## Numbers and definitions

- Test length: one hour [07:20]. Almost 100 players tested the morning of the talk [28:26].
- Validation: three years, 1,500 player scores, about 330 combine participants per year (plus a Super Regional), about 70 percent team participation across all 32 teams [08:52], [09:22].
- Coach ratings on about 24 dimensions after at least a year; about 500 players with performance data [09:54].
- Coaches' scale of about seven points [12:59].
- Correlations (captions read "0 28," "about3," "a0 29," "about 35," "0 22"): about 0.28 [10:24], about 0.3 for the cognitive composite [10:56], about 0.29 for personality [11:26], about 0.35 combined [15:33], 0.22 for decisions under stress [16:03]. The captions garble the decimal points; these are the likeliest readings.
- Top and bottom groups each about 25 percent of the sample [12:27].
- Rated low by coaches 13 percent of the time, good to great 87 percent (high intelligence scorers) [14:01]; 91 percent good to great (strong personality scorers) [15:02].
- Larger penalty sample about 400 players [17:07].
- Clusters: nine profiles from 2014 to 2016 data, shown as z-scores [22:16].

Bust rate 41 percent in the "whole package" cluster and 83 percent in the low cluster [24:19]. A "0%" figure for the six-or-above line in the low cluster is stated at [24:50]; the caption is unclear.

## Summary

The CEO of an athlete-management and analytics company argues that injuries drive wins, and that most teams use load data wrongly. Using base salary as a stand-in for performance, he links lost salary from injuries to wins in the NBA and NFL. He then presents team-level charts where less load, not more, coincided with more injuries, and argues that common thresholds (a one standard deviation change, the 1.5 acute to chronic ratio) fail when checked against a team's own data. He says risk models need pooled, anonymized data and specific questions about pathology, timing and mechanism. Many results are shown only as charts, and the speaker's company is the source.

## Key claims

- Earlier attempts to link injuries to wins failed because counts of injuries or days lost assume every athlete matters equally [01:36], [02:06].
- Base salary is used as a stand-in for contribution because the speaker believes the best talent is paid the most in a salary cap market [02:38].
- Days lost are priced by deducting a day of salary per missed day, then correlated with wins [03:08].
- The speaker says 63 percent of NBA injury spending is on avoidable injuries (ruptures, strains and sprains) [03:39].
- In the NBA, health alone is said to decide about nine wins a year [04:10].
- Injury rates are rising across leagues while time lost shrinks, and prevention spending is not working [05:10].
- More data has meant more decisions but not better ones; people are disillusioned, as with fitness bands [05:40], [06:11].
- A soccer team's higher exposure to high-speed running and explosive efforts coincided with no injuries, and lower exposure with more; the team had been holding athletes back [06:42], [07:13], [07:43].
- Two NFL examples showed more risk with doing less, and for one team the degree of change mattered, not the total [08:13], [08:43].
- Another NFL chart showed the reverse for accelerations: above 200 in a week, injuries were frequent [08:43].
- The common baseball view that a small change in range of motion sharply raises risk is challenged; the speaker says it varies by person, and an increase in hip internal rotation was linked to elbow ligament strain more than the opposite [09:13], [09:43], [10:13].
- A published acute to chronic ratio threshold did not fit any of four rugby teams in one league [10:13], [10:43].
- Each team and each person has a different load signature, including phenotypes that break from too much load, too little, or both [14:15], [14:46].
- Risk tolerance should change with roster and opponent [13:14].
- Good injury models need specific questions about pathology, season phase, practice versus game, and injury mechanism [16:48], [17:18], [17:49].
- The speaker says no one is truly doing injury prediction with machine learning [15:46], [16:17].
- Teams should keep a few core metrics and review them yearly rather than manage a hundred variables [18:51].
- He claims the company helps teams cut days lost to injury by 42 percent [19:21].

## Numbers and definitions

- Correlation of salary-adjusted spending with wins: 0.76 NBA, 0.89 NFL [03:08].
- NBA average spend on injured players: 12.9 million dollars a year; 8.1 million dollars of that avoidable [03:08], [03:39].
- 46.6 million dollars of athlete on court: 40 wins West, 36 East, 0 percent playoff chance; 52 million dollars: 49 or 43 wins, 100 percent chance [03:39], [04:10].
- Share of wins set by health: NFL 25 percent, MLB 9 percent, NHL 12, MLS 15 [04:40]; NBA said as nine wins, "20%" of wins needed for the playoffs [04:10]. The captions say "NFL or NBA" at [04:10], so the 20 percent is likely NBA.
- Soccer team: "above 30 150 meters" of high-speed running over seven days (garbled; the figure is unclear) and more than 390 explosive multi-directional efforts, with no injuries [06:42], [07:13]. A one standard deviation increase was treated as risky [07:43].
- NFL team: above 200 accelerations in seven days, 33 or 34 percent injured (phrase unclear) [08:43].
- Baseball: 180 degrees of motion; a five degree change claimed to raise risk six to seven times [09:13].
- Acute to chronic ratio: 150 percent said to raise risk six or seven times; the speaker's four teams would have lost 8, (garbled), 15 and 26 percent of training [10:43], [11:13]. The top-right value is garbled in the captions.
- Premier League team: 23 injuries a year of 14 days or more; 8 to 12 of the same type [11:44], [12:14].
- Company claims: 42 percent fewer days lost; 25 leagues, five continents; over four years, first annual report last year [19:21], [19:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Salary-weighted availability as a proxy for performance [02:38], [03:08].
- Dose-response charts of weekly load against injury risk, per team [06:42].
- Electronic medical record at the center, every data point statistically related to injury [11:13], [11:44].
- Anonymized aggregation across athletes, split by sport, position and team [12:14].
- Phenotypes of athletes by load response [14:15].
- Annual review of metrics [18:51].

## Limits and open questions

- Chart samples and statistics are not stated; many numbers are partly garbled.
- The salary link is correlational, and using salary as a stand-in for performance is the speaker's assumption.
- Results cover a few teams; the speaker says each team differs, which limits any general rule.
- It is a company presentation; claims such as 42 percent fewer days lost and being the "proven global leader" are the speaker's own [19:21].
- "Infinitely higher" game injury rate is a figure of speech, not a number [16:48], [17:18].
